title: Statistics for Data & ML
description: Summarize data, avoid the correlation/causation trap, understand sampling, and get an intuitive feel for A/B testing.

lessons.title: Describing a Bunch of Numbers
lessons.description: Learn the everyday numbers that summarize a dataset — mean, median, and spread.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can summarize a list of numbers with a few key statistics and explain what each one tells you.

sections.title: 📊 Mean, median, and mode
sections.content:
These three numbers all try to answer "what's typical?" — but they answer it differently.

**Mean** is the average: add everything up, divide by how many there are.
**Median** is the middle value when you sort the data.
**Mode** is the most frequent value.

• Mean is easy to compute but gets pulled around by extreme values
• Median ignores outliers and just cares about the middle
• Mode is useful for categories, not just numbers

```python
data = [20000, 22000, 25000, 24000, 900000]  # one CEO salary in the mix

mean = sum(data) / len(data)
sorted_data = sorted(data)
median = sorted_data[len(data) // 2]

print(mean)    # 198200.0  — dragged way up by the outlier
print(median)  # 24000.0   — much more "typical"
```

sections.title: 📏 Spread: variance and standard deviation
sections.content:
The mean tells you the center, but not how spread out the data is. Two datasets can have the same mean and look completely different.

**Variance** measures the average squared distance from the mean. **Standard deviation** is just the square root of variance, which puts it back into the original units so it's easier to interpret.

• A small standard deviation means values cluster tightly around the mean
• A large standard deviation means values are spread widely
• Standard deviation is the number you'll see reported constantly in ML papers and dashboards

```python
import statistics

scores = [85, 90, 78, 92, 88]
print(statistics.mean(scores))      # 86.6
print(statistics.stdev(scores))     # ~5.5 — scores cluster fairly tightly
```

sections.title: 📈 Reading a distribution shape
sections.content:
Beyond a single center and spread number, it helps to know the *shape* of your data.

• **Symmetric**: values spread evenly on both sides of the mean (like heights)
• **Skewed right**: a long tail of high values pulls the mean above the median (like salaries or house prices)
• **Skewed left**: a long tail of low values pulls the mean below the median

When mean and median are far apart, that's a strong hint your data is skewed — and it's often better to report the median.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Reporting only the mean.** Always pair it with a spread measure (standard deviation) or the median — a mean alone hides whether data is tightly clustered or wildly spread.

**Using mean on skewed data.** For things like income or house prices, the median is usually more representative because it isn't dragged by extreme values.

**Confusing variance and standard deviation.** Variance is in squared units (hard to interpret); standard deviation is in the original units — that's why it's reported more often.

questions.question: A dataset has mean = 50 and median = 30. What does this suggest?
options: The data is symmetric
The data is skewed right (a few very high values)
There's an error in the data
The data has no spread
questions.explanation: When the mean is pulled well above the median, it usually means a few unusually high values are dragging the average up — a right-skewed distribution.

questions.question: Which statistic is most resistant to outliers?
options: Mean
Median
Standard deviation
Sum
questions.explanation: The median only cares about the middle value's position, so extreme values barely affect it. The mean, by contrast, shifts a lot when outliers are added.

questions.question: What does a small standard deviation tell you?
options: The data has a high mean
The values are tightly clustered near the mean
The data is skewed
The dataset is small
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures spread. A small value means most data points sit close to the mean; a large value means they're spread out widely.

questions.question: What is the mode of a dataset?
options: The average of all values
The middle value when sorted
The most frequently occurring value
The difference between the highest and lowest values
questions.explanation: The mode is simply the value (or values) that appears most often in the dataset.

questions.question: What does the range of a dataset measure?
options: The average distance between all pairs of values
The difference between the maximum and minimum values
The most common value
The middle value
questions.explanation: Range is calculated as the maximum value minus the minimum value, giving a simple sense of the data's overall spread.

questions.question: How does a single extreme outlier typically affect the mean of a dataset?
options: It has no effect on the mean at all
It can pull the mean noticeably toward the outlier's value, since every value contributes to the sum
It always pulls the mean toward the median instead
It only affects the mode
questions.explanation: Because the mean sums every value, one extreme outlier can shift it substantially, unlike the median which is far less sensitive to extreme values.

questions.question: When a dataset is heavily skewed, which statistic often gives a more representative sense of the 'typical' value?
options: The mean, since it uses every data point
The median, since it isn't pulled around by extreme values
The range, since it captures the full spread
The mode, since it's always the highest value
questions.explanation: In skewed data, the median tends to better represent a 'typical' value since it isn't distorted by a handful of extreme outliers the way the mean can be.

questions.question: What do quartiles (as in a five-number summary) describe about a dataset?
options: Only the single average value
Points that divide the sorted data into four equal-sized groups, showing its spread and shape
The most frequent value only
Whether the data contains any negative numbers
questions.explanation: Quartiles split sorted data into four equal parts, and together with the min and max form the five-number summary describing the data's distribution and spread.

lessons.title: Correlation Is Not Causation
lessons.description: Understand what correlation actually measures — and why it can trick you into wrong conclusions.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can compute and interpret a correlation coefficient, and explain why a strong correlation doesn't prove one thing causes another.

sections.title: 🔗 What correlation measures
sections.content:
**Correlation** measures how two variables move together, on a scale from -1 to 1.

• **+1** — perfectly move together (as one goes up, so does the other)
• **0** — no linear relationship
• **-1** — perfectly move opposite (as one goes up, the other goes down)

```python
import statistics

hours_studied = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
test_scores =   [50, 55, 65, 70, 80]

# correlation is close to +1 here — more studying, higher scores
```

Correlation only captures *linear* relationships — two variables can be strongly related in a curved way and still show near-zero correlation.

sections.title: 🚫 Why correlation isn't causation
sections.content:
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are correlated — both rise in summer. Does ice cream cause drowning? Obviously not. A hidden third factor, **hot weather**, drives both.

This is called a **confounding variable** — something that influences both things you're measuring, creating a correlation that has nothing to do with cause and effect.

• Two variables can be correlated because one causes the other
• They can be correlated because a third variable causes both
• They can be correlated by pure coincidence, especially in small datasets

sections.title: 🧪 How you'd actually show causation
sections.content:
To claim X *causes* Y, you generally need more than correlation:

• A **controlled experiment** (like an A/B test) where you change X and keep everything else the same
• A plausible **mechanism** explaining how X could affect Y
• Ruling out obvious confounders

This is why ML models trained on correlations can be misleading if used to justify real-world interventions — a model finding "customers who see this banner buy more" doesn't mean the banner *caused* the purchase.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming correlation implies causation.** This is the single most common statistical mistake in headlines and business decks — always ask "could something else explain this?"

**Ignoring confounding variables.** Before concluding X affects Y, ask what else might affect both.

**Trusting correlation on tiny samples.** With very few data points, a strong-looking correlation can appear by pure chance.

questions.question: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer. What best explains this correlation?
options: Ice cream causes drowning
Drowning causes people to buy ice cream
A confounding variable (hot weather) drives both
The correlation is meaningless and should be ignored
questions.explanation: Hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming (and therefore drowning risk). It's a confounding variable creating a correlation with no direct causal link between the two.

questions.question: A correlation coefficient of 0.05 between two variables suggests:
options: A strong positive relationship
A strong negative relationship
Little to no linear relationship
Perfect causation
questions.explanation: A coefficient near 0 means the variables show almost no linear relationship — they don't move together in any consistent linear way.

questions.question: What's generally needed to claim X causes Y, beyond observing they're correlated?
options: A bigger dataset with the same correlation
A controlled experiment or a ruled-out set of confounders
A correlation coefficient closer to 0
Nothing — correlation is sufficient
questions.explanation: Establishing causation typically requires a controlled experiment (changing X while holding other things constant) or strong evidence ruling out other explanations — correlation alone isn't enough.

questions.question: What range of values can a correlation coefficient take?
options: -1 to 1
0 to 1 only
Any real number, with no bounds
questions.explanation: Correlation coefficients range from -1 (perfect negative relationship) to 1 (perfect positive relationship), with 0 indicating no linear relationship.

questions.question: What does a correlation coefficient of exactly -1 indicate?
options: No relationship between the variables at all
A perfect negative linear relationship — as one variable increases, the other decreases in perfect lockstep
A perfect positive linear relationship
The data must contain an error
questions.explanation: A correlation of -1 means the two variables move in perfectly opposite directions in a perfectly linear pattern.

questions.question: On a scatter plot, what would you expect to see for two variables with a strong positive correlation?
options: Points scattered with no visible pattern
Points forming a rough upward-sloping trend, clustered fairly close to a line
Points forming a downward-sloping trend
All points stacked at a single value
questions.explanation: Strong positive correlation shows up visually as points that roughly trend upward together, clustering near an upward-sloping line.

questions.question: What kind of relationship might a correlation coefficient near 0 fail to detect?
options: It always correctly detects every kind of relationship
A strong but nonlinear relationship, such as a U-shaped or curved pattern, since correlation only measures linear association
Any relationship involving negative numbers
Relationships between more than two variables
questions.explanation: Standard correlation coefficients only capture linear relationships, so two variables could have a strong nonlinear (e.g. U-shaped) relationship and still show a correlation near 0.

questions.question: Besides a confounding variable, what's another possibility to rule out before assuming X causes Y from a correlation?
options: Nothing else needs to be considered once correlation is observed
That the causation actually runs in reverse — Y might be causing X instead
That the correlation coefficient was computed using the wrong sign
That the sample size was too large
questions.explanation: Reverse causation — where the presumed effect actually causes the presumed cause — is another explanation that must be ruled out before concluding X causes Y from correlation alone.

lessons.title: Sampling and the Law of Large Numbers
lessons.description: Learn why we sample instead of measuring everything, and why bigger samples give more reliable answers.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why sampling works, what makes a sample biased, and why more data reduces uncertainty.

sections.title: 🎲 Why we sample
sections.content:
You usually can't measure an entire population — every voter, every customer, every possible sensor reading. Instead, you take a **sample**: a smaller, manageable subset, and use it to estimate something about the whole population.

The key requirement: the sample needs to be **representative** of the population you care about. A sample of your most loyal customers won't tell you much about occasional buyers.

sections.title: ⚖️ Sampling bias
sections.content:
**Sampling bias** happens when your sample systematically differs from the population you're trying to understand.

Classic example: a phone survey conducted only during weekday work hours will oversample retirees and undersample people with 9-to-5 jobs — the sample isn't representative of "all adults."

• Random sampling helps avoid bias by giving everyone a fair chance of being included
• Convenience sampling (whoever's easiest to reach) is fast but often badly biased
• In ML, training data that doesn't reflect real-world usage causes models to perform poorly in production

sections.title: 📐 The Law of Large Numbers
sections.content:
The **Law of Large Numbers** says: as your sample size grows, the sample average gets closer and closer to the true population average.

```python
import random

# Flipping a fair coin (true probability of heads = 0.5)
for n in [10, 100, 10000]:
    flips = [random.random() < 0.5 for _ in range(n)]
    print(n, sum(flips) / n)

# With n=10, the fraction might be 0.3 or 0.7 — noisy
# With n=10000, it lands very close to 0.5 — much more stable
```

This is exactly why more training data generally makes a model's learned patterns more reliable — small samples are noisy, large samples average out that noise.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Trusting conclusions from tiny samples.** A pattern in 10 data points can easily be random noise, not a real signal.

**Ignoring how the sample was collected.** A large biased sample is still biased — size alone doesn't fix a bad sampling method.

**Confusing "large sample" with "representative sample."** You need both size and a fair collection process.

questions.question: A survey only calls landline phones during weekday afternoons. What's the main problem?
options: The sample is too large
The sample is biased — it oversamples people home during weekday afternoons
The Law of Large Numbers doesn't apply to phone surveys
There is no problem
questions.explanation: This sampling method systematically excludes people who work during the day or don't use landlines, so the sample won't represent the full population fairly.

questions.question: According to the Law of Large Numbers, as sample size increases, the sample average:
options: Becomes less reliable
Gets closer to the true population average
Always equals the population average exactly
Becomes impossible to compute
questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce random noise, so the sample average converges toward — but doesn't necessarily exactly equal — the true population average.

questions.question: Why is a large but biased sample still a problem?
options: Large samples are always unbiased by definition
Size only reduces random noise — it doesn't fix systematic bias in how the sample was collected
Bias only matters in small samples
It isn't a problem
questions.explanation: More data averages out random noise, but if the collection method is systematically skewed, a bigger sample just gives you a more confident, precise version of the same biased answer.

questions.question: What is the general purpose of random sampling?
options: To guarantee every measurement is identical
To give a subset of the population a fair chance of being selected, so the sample better represents the whole population
To intentionally favor certain groups over others
To reduce the amount of data collected to zero
questions.explanation: Random sampling aims to select subjects in a way that doesn't systematically favor any group, so the resulting sample better reflects the full population.

questions.question: How does increasing sample size generally affect the precision of an estimate?
options: Larger samples always make estimates less precise
Larger samples generally reduce the random variability of the estimate, making it more precise
Sample size has no effect on precision at all
Precision only depends on the population size, not the sample size
questions.explanation: As sample size grows, the estimate's random fluctuation tends to shrink, generally yielding a more precise (less variable) estimate of the true population value.

questions.question: What's the difference between a population and a sample in statistics?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
The population is the entire group of interest; the sample is a subset actually measured or surveyed
A sample is always larger than the population
Population only applies to countries, not datasets
questions.explanation: The population is the complete group you want to understand, while the sample is the smaller subset you actually collect data from to estimate things about that population.

questions.question: What is sampling error?
options: A mistake made only when using biased sampling methods
The natural difference between a sample statistic and the true population value, arising just from having measured a subset rather than everyone
An error that can be completely eliminated by using any sample
A synonym for sampling bias
questions.explanation: Sampling error is the expected discrepancy between what a sample shows and the true population value, simply because a subset rather than the entire population was measured — distinct from bias, which comes from a flawed sampling method.

questions.question: Why does it matter whether a sample is representative of the population it's drawn from?
options: Representativeness has no bearing on the conclusions drawn
Conclusions drawn from an unrepresentative sample may not generalize to the broader population, even if the sample itself is analyzed correctly
A representative sample is only needed for very small datasets
Any sample, representative or not, generalizes equally well
questions.explanation: If a sample doesn't reflect the population's true composition, conclusions drawn from it can be misleading when applied back to that broader population, regardless of how carefully the sample itself was analyzed.

lessons.title: A/B Testing and Hypothesis Testing Intuition
lessons.description: Get a practical, intuitive feel for how A/B tests decide whether a difference is real or just noise.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what an A/B test is checking for and what a p-value intuitively represents.

sections.title: 🅰️🅱️ What an A/B test does
sections.content:
An **A/B test** compares two versions of something — like two website button colors — by showing each version to a different random group of users and measuring the outcome (like click rate).

• Group A sees the current version (the **control**)
• Group B sees the new version (the **treatment**)
• You compare the results to see if B performs meaningfully better

Randomly assigning users to each group is what makes this a real experiment — not just an observation — because it rules out most confounding variables.

sections.title: ❓ The core question: is the difference real?
sections.content:
Suppose button A converts 10% of visitors and button B converts 11%. Is B actually better, or did it just get luckier this time by random chance?

This is where **hypothesis testing** comes in. You start by assuming there's *no real difference* between A and B (this is called the **null hypothesis**), then ask: "if that were true, how surprising would a gap this big be?"

sections.title: 📉 What a p-value intuitively means
sections.content:
A **p-value** answers: "if A and B were truly identical, what's the chance we'd see a difference at least this large just from random luck?"

• A small p-value (like 0.01) means this result would be surprising if there were no real difference — so you lean toward believing B genuinely performs differently
• A large p-value (like 0.6) means a gap this size is unsurprising even with no real difference — not enough evidence to conclude anything

A common (if somewhat arbitrary) threshold is p < 0.05 to call a result "statistically significant."

```python
# Conceptually — not exact code, just the idea:
# 1. Run the experiment, measure conversion rates for A and B
# 2. Ask: "how likely is this gap if there's truly no difference?"
# 3. If that likelihood (the p-value) is very small, the difference
#    is probably real, not just noise
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Stopping the test too early.** Small sample sizes make random noise look like a real effect — let the test collect enough data first.

**Treating statistical significance as proof of a big effect.** A tiny, practically meaningless difference can still be "statistically significant" with a huge sample size.

**Running many comparisons and only reporting the one that looked significant.** If you test 20 button colors, one will look better than the rest by pure chance — that doesn't mean it truly is better.

questions.question: In an A/B test, why is randomly assigning users to group A or B important?
options: It makes the test run faster
It helps ensure the two groups are comparable, so differences in outcome can be attributed to A vs B rather than other factors
It's not important — any grouping method works equally well
It guarantees B will win
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances out other factors (like device type, time of day, user habits) between the two groups, so any observed difference is more likely due to the change itself rather than a confounding factor.

questions.question: A p-value of 0.6 for an A/B test result suggests:
options: Strong evidence that B is better than A
The observed difference could easily happen by random chance even if A and B are truly the same
The test was run incorrectly
B is definitely worse than A
questions.explanation: A large p-value means the observed gap isn't surprising under the assumption of no real difference — there isn't strong evidence of a genuine effect.

questions.question: Why is stopping an A/B test too early risky?
options: Small samples are noisy, so an early lead can easily be random chance rather than a real effect
Early results are always more accurate
It has no risk at all
It violates the null hypothesis
questions.explanation: With few data points collected, random fluctuations can easily create a misleading lead for one version — waiting for a larger, more stable sample reduces that risk.

questions.question: What does the null hypothesis typically state in an A/B test?
options: That B is definitely better than A
That there is no real difference between A and B — any observed difference is just due to random chance
That the test must be run again
That A is definitely better than B
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis is the default assumption that A and B perform the same, and the test looks for evidence strong enough to reject that assumption.

questions.question: What does a small p-value, like 0.01, suggest about an observed difference between A and B?
options: The difference is almost certainly just random noise
The observed difference would be unlikely to occur by chance alone if A and B were truly the same, suggesting a real effect
The test was set up incorrectly
B is definitely worse than A
questions.explanation: A small p-value indicates the observed result would be quite unlikely under the assumption that A and B are the same, which is often taken as evidence of a genuine difference.

questions.question: What's the difference between statistical significance and practical significance?
options: They always mean the exact same thing
Statistical significance means the difference is unlikely due to chance; practical significance asks whether that difference is actually large enough to matter in real terms
Practical significance is a stricter version of statistical significance
Statistical significance only applies to A/B tests, not other experiments
questions.explanation: A tiny, real difference can be statistically significant with enough data, yet still be too small to matter practically — the two concepts answer different questions.

questions.question: Why does an A/B test typically need a control group?
options: It doesn't — only the new version needs to be tested
The control group (A) provides a baseline to compare the new version (B) against, isolating the effect of the change
Control groups are only needed in medical experiments
It's required purely for legal reasons, not statistical ones
questions.explanation: Comparing group B against a control group A establishes a baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to the change being tested rather than unrelated factors.

questions.question: Why might a very small sample size make it hard to detect a real but modest difference between A and B?
options: Small samples always detect every difference easily
Small samples have more random noise, which can mask a real but modest effect, leading to a large p-value even when a true difference exists
Sample size has no bearing on a test's ability to detect differences
It only matters if the effect is extremely large
questions.explanation: With few observations, random variation can be large relative to the true effect size, making it hard to distinguish a genuine but modest difference from mere chance.
